summary.text: The Underground Railroad was an organized network of secret routes and safe houses that helped fugitive slaves escape to the abolitionist Northern United States and Eastern Canada.
The network, primarily the work of free and enslaved African Americans, was assisted by abolitionists, and those who fled and those who helped were called passengers and conductors.
One estimate suggests about 100,000 slaves had escaped to freedom through the network by 1850, and separately an estimated 30,000 to 40,000 settled in Canada.

facts.label: When it organized
facts.value: In the 1780s, among abolitionist societies in the North

facts.label: Passengers and conductors
facts.value: Escapees were passengers; those who aided them were conductors

facts.label: First printed use
facts.value: Thomas Smallwood used the term on August 10, 1842

facts.label: Estimated escapes
facts.value: About 100,000 slaves by 1850, by one estimate

facts.label: Settled in Canada
facts.value: An estimated 30,000 to 40,000 fugitives, half in 1850–1860

items.prompt: How did the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 affect efforts to help escapees?

options.label: It stirred abolitionists to help more, which grew anti-slavery societies and the network
It stopped most helpers, who feared arrest and ended their work
It shifted the work to Southern states, where officials ran the routes
It had no effect, since free states ignored all of it

items.explain: The law made recapture easier and created an eagerness among abolitionists to help enslaved people, resulting in the growth of anti-slavery societies and the Underground Railroad.

items.prompt: The name 'Underground Railroad' began as a joke. What was it mocking?

options.label: Abolitionists' habit of meeting in cellars at night
Enslavers' astonishment at how many people were escaping
The slow trains that carried fugitives north
Southern politicians' plans to build rail lines

items.explain: Thomas Smallwood used the term to mock enslavers' astonishment at the numbers escaping, quoting a constable who said they must travel by 'steam balloon' or 'underground rail-road'.

items.prompt: Under the Compromise of 1850, a man suspected of being a fugitive is hauled before an official. What is true of his position?

options.label: He may call witnesses, and the court must wait for them
He is protected until his accuser pays a bond
He cannot defend himself in court, which makes proving he is free difficult
He is free to go if a state official refuses to act

items.explain: The law deprived people suspected of being slaves of the right to defend themselves in court and required sparse documentation to claim a person was a fugitive.

items.prompt: Someone assumes every route of the Underground Railroad ran to Canada. What is a good correction?

options.label: Routes ran only to free states, and none went outside the country
Routes ran only east toward the Atlantic and then by ship
Routes all ended in Canada, but some began in Mexico
Routes also led to the Caribbean, western and Indian territories, and into Mexico

items.explain: Routes went north to free states and Canada, but also to the Caribbean, western territories, Indian territories, and south into Mexico.

items.prompt: How did Southern politicians often talk about the number of escapes?

options.label: They exaggerated the numbers and blamed Northerners for interfering with property rights
They played them down and said fugitives usually returned
They blamed Canada's government for sending agents south
They praised the escapes as proof the system was working

items.explain: Southern politicians often exaggerated the number of escaped slaves and blamed Northerners interfering with Southern property rights.

items.prompt: Escapees spoke of a 'Gospel train' heading to 'the Promised Land'. Where did that name point?

options.label: To Mexico, where slavery had been abolished
To Canada, which many treated as their final destination
To Washington, D.C., where abolitionists published
To Florida, which was a Spanish possession

items.explain: The railroad was called the 'freedom train' or 'Gospel train', heading toward Heaven or the Promised Land, i.e. Canada.
